profile.name: Rueda de Casino
profile.tagline: Cuban salsa circle dance with partner swaps called by a dancing leader.
profile.insight: In 2017, 230 groups worldwide performed Rueda de Casino simultaneously, showcasing stark differences between original Cuban and Miami styles.
profile.profile: Rueda de Casino originated in Havana, Cuba, in the 1950s at Club Casino Deportivo. Couples form a circle (rueda) and dance synchronized figures called out by a dancing leader (líder) inside the circle. The dance fuses Cuban Son, Cha Cha Cha, Mambo, and Rumba Guaguancó, featuring continuous partner exchanges and hand signals. It spread globally via Cuban emigrants, evolving distinct Miami and Cuban styles.
profile.profile_long: Rueda de Casino emerged in Havana, Cuba, around 1956 at the Club Casino Deportivo, where multiple couples formed a circle to dance synchronized salsa figures called out by a leader who danced within the circle. The dance evolved from Cuban Urban Son and Cha Cha Cha, incorporating partner turns from Mambo and Rumba Guaguancó, and is distinct for its improvisational use of Afro-Cuban dance vocabulary, especially among Afro-Cuban dancers who integrate folkloric gestures and references to dances for Orishas. The circular formation, or rueda, requires at least two couples but can include many, sometimes forming concentric circles in larger venues. The caller, known as the cantante or líder, improvises the sequence of moves, which include partner swaps and are often accompanied by hand signals to aid communication in noisy settings. Fundamental moves include Dame, Enchufla, Vacila, and Sombrero, each with specific hand signs, such as tapping the head for Sombrero. The dance originally accompanied Cuban Son montuno and guaracha rhythms before becoming associated with salsa and timba music. After the Cuban Revolution, emigrants brought Rueda de Casino to Miami, where Rene Gueits structured a disco-like variant removing many Afro-Cuban elements, creating a Miami style distinct from the original Cuban form. The dance has since spread worldwide, with large flash mobs and record-breaking gatherings, including a 2017 event with 230 groups dancing simultaneously, highlighting stylistic differences. The dance is social and improvisational, with over 300 recognized figures varying by region and teacher, and is performed in Spanish with some Spanglish terms. Rueda de Casino is a living tradition reflecting Cuban cultural identity and community.

sections.origins_and_history: Rueda de Casino originated in Havana, Cuba, in the early 1950s, first danced at Club Casino Deportivo around 1956. It developed from Cuban Urban Son, Cha Cha Cha, Mambo, and Rumba Guaguancó. The circular group dance with partner swapping was called 'Rueda del Casino' and became popular in Havana clubs and on television by the late 1970s. Cuban emigrants brought it to Miami during the Mariel boatlift, where it evolved into a structured, disco-influenced Miami style. The dance spread globally, with international flash mobs in 2014 and 2017 involving hundreds of groups worldwide.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Couples form a circle (rueda) holding closed dance position. A caller (líder) inside the circle calls out moves, which the dancers execute simultaneously. Moves include partner swaps and turns, often accompanied by hand signals. The dance starts from 'al Medio' (closed hold stepping in and out) or 'Guapea' (stepping forward on inside foot, backward on outside foot tangent to the circle). Fundamental moves include Dame (gentleman fetches partner to right), Enchufla (partner turn and swap), Vacila, and Sombrero (caller taps head). The sequence is improvised, requiring dancers to listen and watch closely. Technique details such as footwork counts and posture are not fully described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: Rueda de Casino is danced to Cuban Son montuno, guaracha, and later salsa and timba music. The tempo is typically salsa tempo but exact BPM is not specified. Instruments traditionally include Cuban percussion and brass typical of salsa and timba bands. Vocal style is lively, often with call-and-response. The music supports the circular, energetic, and rhythmic partner exchanges.
sections.costume_and_setting: Danced socially in clubs, dance studios, and outdoor venues. Traditional Cuban dancers sometimes wear white clothing, especially older groups in Havana. The dance circle can vary in size from two couples to large groups forming concentric circles. No specific ceremonial costume is described. The setting is informal and social.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Rueda de Casino is a social dance reflecting Cuban cultural identity and community. It is performed at social gatherings, dance events, and festivals. The dance fosters group cohesion through synchronized movements and partner exchanges. It is not described as a sacred or ritual dance.
sections.notable_figures: Rene Gueits, founder of Salsa Lovers in Miami (1994), structured the Miami style of Rueda de Casino, modifying the original Cuban style by removing Afro-Cuban elements. Cuban dancers and groups on the island and abroad have preserved and shared the original style.
sections.regional_variants: Two main styles: original Cuban style with Afro-Cuban improvisation and Miami style with disco influences and structured choreography. Variations exist between Cuban towns and teachers, with different names for moves and figures. Other Rueda forms inspired by Rueda de Casino include Rueda de Bachata and Swing Rueda.
sections.lineage: Descended from Cuban Urban Son and Cha Cha Cha, incorporating partner turns from Mambo and Rumba Guaguancó. Shares Afro-Cuban dance vocabulary and gestures. Influenced by folkloric dances and popular Cuban social dances.

basic_steps: Form a circle with couples holding closed dance position
Start with 'al Medio' step: step in and out of the circle
Or start with 'Guapea': step forward on inside foot, backward on outside foot tangent to the circle
Listen for caller's move and watch hand signals
Execute called moves simultaneously, including partner swaps and turns
teaching.formation: Circle (rueda) of couples, sometimes multiple concentric circles
teaching.level_notes: Beginners start with basic moves like Dame and Enchufla; intermediate and advanced levels include complex figures and improvisations.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Salsa and timba rhythms with clave-based percussion
music_profile.vocal_style: Call-and-response vocals typical of salsa and timba
music_profile.musical_form: Typically montuno sections with repeated rhythmic patterns supporting dancing

movement_profile.posture: Upright with closed dance hold; dancers face partner within the circle
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Hand signals accompany calls; arms used for partner turns and exchanges
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Natural salsa hip movement; torso rotates with turns
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Circular formation with couples rotating positions during partner swaps
movement_profile.partnering: Closed hold; frequent partner exchanges directed by caller
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Syncopated salsa rhythm, moderate to fast tempo

signature_moves.name: Dame
signature_moves.description: Gentleman fetches the partner to his right, initiating a partner swap

signature_moves.name: Enchufla
signature_moves.description: Partner turns inside the circle and swaps places with the caller's right-side partner

signature_moves.name: Vacila
signature_moves.description: A playful move involving a turn and a pause

signature_moves.name: Sombrero
signature_moves.description: Caller taps the top of the head as a hand signal; dancers perform a specific turn

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Levels range from basic to ultra advanced with complex figures; jumps not described
movement_profile.difficulty: beginner to advanced depending on figures
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid missing calls; maintain spatial awareness to prevent collisions; respect cultural origins by not altering Afro-Cuban elements in original style

episode_brief.title_hook: Rueda de Casino: The Cuban Salsa Circle That Spins the World
episode_brief.logline: Discover how a Havana club dance from the 1950s became a global salsa phenomenon where dancers swap partners in a spinning circle.
beats: Opening scene at Club Casino Deportivo in 1950s Havana with couples forming a circle
Close-up on the caller dancing inside the circle calling moves like Dame and Enchufla
Historical footage/photos of Cuban emigrants bringing Rueda to Miami
Contrast Miami style with original Cuban style in split-screen
Flash mob scenes from 2014 and 2017 international Rueda events
Demonstration of hand signals and partner swaps
Interview with a Cuban Rueda elder and Miami instructor
Closing with a large rueda circle dancing energetically

lesson_ladder.goal: Learn basic steps and simple calls
Master additional figures and improve synchronization

drills: Learn advanced figures from master level
